title: Patanjali's first word: now
hookLine: a legend says the yoga teacher fell as a tiny serpent into his mother's joined palms; his book opens with one small word
carry: yoga is the stilling of the mind
tomorrow: when the mind goes quiet, who is left?
last: TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT — BLOCK A, DONE.

cards: A yoga class at a gym: mats, mirrors, someone holding a long, shaking plank.

In some studios there's a small statue up front, and if you look closely, the figure is half man and half serpent, with a hood of snake heads over him. That's Patanjali, the name the Yoga Sutras are gathered under.
And Hindus tell a story about how he came.

teach.b: A woman named Gonika, the legend goes, a seeker herself, was praying for a son she could pass her learning to.
At sunrise she stood in the water and cupped her hands to offer water to the sun, and a tiny serpent dropped into her open palms. Pata, fallen; anjali, joined palms: Patanjali.

The serpent, in the story, is Adishesha, the great snake Vishnu rests on, come down to teach. It's a legend, not history, but it says what Hindus believe about this book: it was given, not invented. The book agrees.
Sutra 1.1: atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha, now, marks a beginning: here the real subject starts.
A traditional verse says om and atha were the first sounds from the creator's throat, so both are lucky words to begin with. Anushasanam, commentators say, is teaching that comes after: handed down.
Then sutra 1.2 gives the definition: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah.

teach.h: A DARSHANA: THE POINT IS THE MIND.
teach.b: Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Chitta, the mind. Vritti, a turning, like water in an eddy.

teach.h: YOGA IS THE STILLING OF THE TURNINGS.
teach.b: Nirodha, stilling. Only three of the sutras even deal with posture. In Hindu tradition, yoga is one of the six classical darshanas, ways of seeing, and its aim is a mind so still that the seer can rest in itself.

That's why a class in India may open with om and a bow to Patanjali, and why many students still chant a verse to him before study, honoring him for clearing the mind with yoga, speech with grammar and the body with medicine.
The stretch is welcome. The point is the mind.

how: Students of yoga in many Hindu lineages begin study of the Yoga Sutras with an invocation to Patanjali and by chanting 1.1 and 1.2, often with Vyasa's classic commentary, and treat 1.2 as the definition the whole text unfolds.

games.q: Sam's gym yoga teacher calls yoga 'a full-body workout.' by Patanjali's second sutra, what is yoga?
o: the stilling of the turnings of the mind.
games.why: yogash chitta vritti nirodhah, sutra 1.2. the poses are welcome; the point is a mind whose whirling settles.

practice: Begin the way Patanjali's students do. If you pray, join your palms and say om once, softly; if you don't, just join your palms. Then sit upright and watch the turnings: a thought arrives, swirls, goes.
Each time you notice you've been carried off, say one word silently, now, atha, not as a scolding but as a fresh start, and settle back on the breath. Every return is the first sutra, said again.

wordCard.voice: Now. The first word of the Yoga Sutras, atha: the teaching begins here, and so does the practice, every time you come back.

orig.note: Sanskrit atha: now. the first word of the Yoga Sutras, a traditional mark of a beginning.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga is the stilling of the mind. And every return is atha, now. That's day four hundred thirty.
